plan.topic: EASD 2026 study of 313,145 adults (UK Biobank + Copenhagen): people with a BMI of 25–26.9 and high remnant cholesterol or low-grade inflammation had heart-disease risk similar to groups who qualify for GLP-1s today
plan.angle: 'Your BMI isn't the whole story.' Start with how GLP-1 eligibility works now: BMI thresholds plus weight-related conditions, and the SELECT population (adults with established heart disease and overweight or obesity, without diabetes). Then the new finding. Among 313,145 adults, 23,134 developed coronary heart disease over 10–18 years. About 44–48% of those with a BMI of 25–26.9 had high remnant cholesterol or inflammation (CRP), and their risk looked similar to groups who are eligible today. Explain what remnant cholesterol and CRP are and how they're measured. Give the questions to bring to your doctor. Limits, said clearly: this is an observational risk study presented at a conference, it did not test GLP-1 drugs, it doesn't show that these people would benefit, and trials are needed. Avoid saying 'millions should be on GLP-1s'. Use the analysed sample size and the source's exact figures throughout.
plan.working_title: Not 'Heavy Enough' for a GLP-1? Two Blood Markers That May Matter More Than BMI
plan.why: Presented at EASD, which opens today. Low competition, and almost no creator videos yet. Fills the 'who may benefit' pillar with plenty of depth for 10+ minutes.

package.description:
Same BMI, different heart risk. A study presented at EASD 2026 followed 313,145 adults and suggests that BMI-based GLP-1 eligibility rules may miss people whose cholesterol and inflammation markers point to higher heart risk.

Quick answer: In data presented at EASD 2026, researchers followed 313,145 adults from the UK Biobank and Copenhagen cohorts for up to 18 years; 23,134 developed coronary heart disease. Among people with a BMI of 25–26.9, about 44–48% had high remnant cholesterol or elevated CRP (a marker of low-grade inflammation), and their risk of coronary heart disease looked similar to groups who already qualify for GLP-1 medicines today. This is an observational study presented at a conference — it did not test GLP-1 drugs and does not prove this group would benefit from them.

What you'll learn:
• How GLP-1 eligibility works today: BMI thresholds, weight-related conditions, and the SELECT trial population
• What "remnant cholesterol" is and how to estimate it from a standard cholesterol panel
• What CRP measures and how it flags low-grade inflammation
• The exact numbers behind the 313,145-person EASD 2026 study
• The key limits of this research, stated clearly
• Questions worth bringing to your doctor about your own risk

This video is for education only and isn't medical advice. GLP-1 medicines are prescription treatments. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether one is right for you, and don't start, stop or change any medicine without them.

2. SELECT trial: Semaglutide and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Obesity without Diabetes (NEJM, 2023): https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307563
3. FDA approves semaglutide to reduce heart risk in adults with obesity or overweight (FDA, 2024): https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-treatment-reduce-risk-serious-heart-problems-specifically-adults-obesity-or
4. Remnant cholesterol as a causal risk factor for ischemic heart disease (JACC, 2013): https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2012.08.1026
5. CRP and risk of coronary heart disease: individual participant meta-analysis (Lancet, 2010): https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(09)61717-7

script.working_title: Not 'Heavy Enough' for a GLP-1? Two Blood Markers BMI Can Miss
script.hook_pattern: Open loop, set up with a visceral 'you' scenario: two people with the same BMI and very different hidden heart risk, and one marker you can work out from a test you've already had (paid off in 'The hidden cholesterol')

scenes.narration: Two people. Same height, same weight, same BMI of twenty-six. On paper, neither one meets today's weight-based criteria for a GLP-1 medicine.

visual.stock_query: two identical cartoon people on scales

scenes.retention_device: Pattern interrupt: two identical people, a question the viewer can't answer yet

scenes.narration: But a huge new study suggests their heart risk could be very different. For one of them, it may look a lot like the risk of people who do qualify today.

visual.stock_query: one cartoon heart glowing warning red

scenes.retention_device: Curiosity gap: which one, and why?

scenes.narration: The difference showed up in two blood markers. And one of them, you can probably work out from a cholesterol test you've already had.

visual.stock_query: cholesterol lab report with magnifying glass

scenes.retention_device: Main open loop planted: the marker hiding in your cholesterol test (paid off in scene s34)

scenes.narration: By the end of this video, you'll know what those two markers are, how to spot them on your results, and exactly what to ask your doctor.
You'll also hear what this study can't tell us. Because that part matters just as much as the headline.

visual.stock_query: cartoon scientist holding fine print scroll

scenes.retention_device: Second open loop: the study's limits (paid off in 'The fine print')

scenes.narration: So first, how do doctors decide who gets a GLP-1 medicine for weight today? Mostly, it starts with one number: your body mass index, or BMI.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter reset with a direct question

scenes.narration: In the US, the weight-management versions of semaglutide and tirzepatide are approved for adults with a BMI of thirty or more.

visual.stock_query: big BMI dial pointing to thirty

scenes.narration: Or a BMI of twenty-seven or more, plus at least one weight-related condition, like high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, or high cholesterol.

visual.stock_query: three health condition icons in a row

scenes.retention_device: Sets up the 27 line that the study sits just below

scenes.narration: In the UK, the NHS follows NICE criteria, which are stricter, and which use lower BMI thresholds for people from some ethnic backgrounds.

visual.stock_query: UK map with clipboard of criteria

scenes.retention_device: Quick contrast keeps UK viewers in

scenes.narration: Then there's a heart approval. In twenty twenty-four, the FDA approved semaglutide to lower the risk of heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death in adults with established cardiovascular disease and either overweight or obesity.
scenes.retention_device: New angle: eligibility based on heart risk, not just weight

scenes.narration: That approval was based on SELECT: a trial of seventeen thousand, six hundred and four adults aged forty-five or older, with established cardiovascular disease, like a past heart attack or stroke, a BMI of twenty-seven or more, and no diabetes.

visual.stat_label: adults with cardiovascular disease in SELECT
visual.stock_query: crowd of cartoon adults with heart badges

scenes.narration: Over an average of about three years, major heart events hit six point five percent of the semaglutide group, versus eight percent on placebo. That's a twenty percent relative drop, or about one and a half percentage points in absolute terms.

visual.stat_label: relative risk of major heart events
visual.stock_query: two bar columns heart events comparison

scenes.retention_device: Surprising stat, shown as both relative and absolute

scenes.narration: Notice the pattern. Outside of type 2 diabetes and a few specific conditions, most doors into these medicines have a BMI number on them. And for a lot of people, the number that matters is twenty-seven.
scenes.retention_device: But/therefore pivot: the line itself becomes the question

scenes.narration: So what about someone sitting just under that line, at twenty-five or twenty-six? That's exactly who this new study zoomed in on.

visual.stock_query: person standing just below height line

scenes.narration: The research is being presented at the twenty twenty-six annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes, known as EASD, in Milan.
The team, led by Dr. Karen Hvid at Copenhagen University Hospital in Herlev, drew on two huge, long-running health studies: UK Biobank, and the Copenhagen General Population Study in Denmark.

visual.stock_query: UK and Denmark flags with data files

scenes.retention_device: Credibility builder before the big number

scenes.narration: In total, they analyzed three hundred thirteen thousand, one hundred forty-five adults. All had a BMI of twenty-five or more, and none had coronary heart disease or diabetes when the study began.

visual.stock_query: huge crowd of tiny cartoon people

scenes.narration: They followed them for up to fifteen to eighteen years, depending on the study. Over that time, twenty-three thousand, one hundred thirty-four people developed coronary heart disease.
That's the kind of heart disease where plaque narrows the arteries feeding your heart muscle. It can cause chest pain, or lead to a heart attack.

visual.stock_query: cartoon artery pipe with plaque buildup

scenes.retention_device: Quick explainer keeps everyone on board

scenes.narration: Now the key group: people with a BMI of twenty-five to twenty-six point nine. Overweight by the standard definition, but below that twenty-seven line.

visual.stock_query: spotlight on small group below line

scenes.narration: The researchers looked at two things in their blood. Remnant cholesterol. And C-reactive protein, or CRP, a marker of low-grade inflammation.
scenes.retention_device: Names the two markers; explanation held for later chapters

scenes.narration: And here's the surprise. In that BMI range, forty-four percent of people in the Copenhagen study, and forty-eight percent in UK Biobank, had high remnant cholesterol, low-grade inflammation, or both.

visual.stat_label: BMI 25–26.9: high remnant cholesterol, CRP, or both

scenes.narration: That's close to half. Not a rare edge case, but a big slice of people that BMI alone wouldn't flag for a GLP-1.
scenes.retention_device: Reframes the stat so it lands

scenes.narration: And for those people, the risk of coronary heart disease looked similar to groups who already qualify for GLP-1 medicines today.

visual.stock_query: two heart risk gauges side by side

scenes.retention_device: Core finding delivered, first half of cold-open loop paid off

scenes.narration: Put simply: two people with the same BMI might carry very different heart risk. And routine blood tests could help tell them apart.

visual.stock_query: twin cartoon people different blood colors

scenes.retention_device: Callback to the two people from the hook

scenes.narration: So what exactly are these two markers? Let's start with the one that's hiding in plain sight.
You've probably heard of LDL, the so-called bad cholesterol, and HDL, the so-called good one. Remnant cholesterol is the one most people never hear about.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter reset with a character-style setup

scenes.narration: Picture your bloodstream as a delivery network. Fat-carrying particles packed with triglycerides drive around, dropping off fuel to your muscles and tissues.

visual.stock_query: delivery trucks driving through blood vessel

scenes.narration: What's left after the drop-off are smaller, leftover particles that still carry cholesterol. That leftover cholesterol is your remnant cholesterol.

visual.stock_query: small empty trucks carrying leftover boxes

scenes.narration: Researchers think these leftover particles can get into artery walls and help build plaque, a bit like LDL does.

visual.stock_query: small particles sticking to pipe wall

scenes.narration: Copenhagen researchers have studied this for years. In a twenty thirteen genetic study, people born with higher remnant cholesterol had more heart disease, pointing toward a causal role, not just a coincidence.

visual.stock_query: DNA strand next to cartoon heart

scenes.narration: So a normal LDL doesn't automatically mean every cholesterol-related risk is covered.

visual.myth: Normal LDL means all cholesterol risk is covered
visual.fact: Remnant cholesterol is linked to heart risk too
visual.stock_query: LDL character with checkmark and question

scenes.narration: Now, here's the part I promised at the start. You probably don't need a special test to estimate it.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop begins

scenes.narration: Grab a standard cholesterol panel. Take your total cholesterol. Subtract your LDL. Then subtract your HDL. What's left is an estimate of your remnant cholesterol. Just keep all three numbers in the same units.
scenes.retention_device: Main loop paid off with an actionable formula

scenes.narration: One catch: many labs calculate LDL from the other numbers instead of measuring it. So treat this as a rough estimate, and go over it with your doctor rather than diagnosing yourself.

The newest US cholesterol guideline, from twenty twenty-six, now recognizes these leftover particles as part of heart risk. And it flags triglycerides that stay at one hundred seventy-five milligrams per deciliter or higher as a risk-enhancing factor. That's about two millimoles per liter.

visual.stat_label: persistent triglycerides (about 2 mmol/L): a US risk enhancer

scenes.retention_device: Concrete number the viewer can check

scenes.narration: That's marker number one. Marker number two isn't about fat at all. It's about fire.
Inflammation is your immune system's alarm. A sprained ankle, a sore throat: it's loud, it's short, and then it switches off.

visual.stock_query: alarm bell ringing then turning off

scenes.narration: But sometimes a quieter alarm keeps humming in the background for months or even years. That's low-grade inflammation.

visual.stock_query: small alarm humming in background room

scenes.narration: The usual way to measure it is C-reactive protein, a protein your liver releases when inflammation is present. For heart risk, doctors use a sensitive version called high-sensitivity CRP.
scenes.retention_device: Clear explainer: what it is and how it's measured

scenes.narration: A major twenty ten analysis pooled more than one hundred sixty thousand people from fifty-four studies. Higher CRP went along with higher coronary heart disease risk.
But that link shrank considerably once other risk factors, like smoking, blood pressure and cholesterol, were taken into account. So CRP is a clue, not a verdict.
Current US cholesterol guidelines treat a high-sensitivity CRP of two milligrams per liter or more, when it stays high on repeat testing with no other explanation, as a risk-enhancing factor.

visual.stat_label: hs-CRP on repeat tests: a risk enhancer

scenes.narration: One practical tip: a cold, an injury or a flare-up can push CRP up for a while. A CDC and American Heart Association statement suggested averaging two tests, about two weeks apart, when you're well.

visual.stock_query: two calendar dates two weeks apart

scenes.narration: And inflammation isn't just a bystander. In the CANTOS trial, a drug that targeted inflammation, without lowering cholesterol, modestly reduced repeat heart events in people with a past heart attack and high CRP.

visual.stock_query: firefighter cooling small flame in artery

scenes.narration: So now we have two markers: leftover cholesterol, and a slow-burning alarm. And this is where GLP-1 medicines come back into the story.
Remember SELECT? Researchers later asked a pointed question: did semaglutide protect hearts only because people lost weight?

visual.stock_query: scale with a big question mark

scenes.retention_device: Chapter reset with a question to the viewer

scenes.narration: In a prespecified analysis published in The Lancet in twenty twenty-four, the heart benefit showed up across the range of starting BMI, and it didn't seem to depend much on how much weight people lost, though a smaller waist may explain part of it.

visual.stock_query: hearts protected across different body sizes

scenes.narration: That hints that something beyond weight loss may be at work. And in the STEP 1 trial, semaglutide also lowered CRP and improved blood fats like triglycerides.

visual.stock_query: arrows lowering flame and fat droplets

scenes.retention_device: Connects the markers to the medicine

scenes.narration: So it's reasonable to wonder whether markers like these could help identify people who might benefit, even below today's BMI cutoffs.

visual.stock_query: thinking cartoon doctor with blood test

scenes.retention_device: Hypothesis stated as a question, not a claim

scenes.narration: But, and this is a big but, wondering isn't knowing. Which brings us to the fine print.
scenes.retention_device: Pays off the second loop from the cold open

scenes.narration: First: this is an observational study. It tracked who developed heart disease. It didn't give anyone a treatment.
So it shows a link between these markers and risk. It can't prove the markers themselves caused the heart disease.
Second, and most important: it didn't test GLP-1 medicines at all. Nobody in this analysis was given semaglutide or tirzepatide as part of the study.

visual.stock_query: empty pill box with question mark

scenes.narration: So it can't tell us whether people with a BMI of twenty-five or twenty-six and these markers would actually benefit. Similar risk doesn't automatically mean similar benefit.

visual.myth: This study shows GLP-1s help people with BMI 25–26.9
visual.fact: It measured heart risk; it didn't test any treatment

scenes.narration: Third, it's a conference presentation. Those are usually a first look, with fewer details than a full journal paper, like the exact cutoffs used and how every factor was adjusted for.

visual.stock_query: conference poster next to thick journal

scenes.narration: Fourth, both cohorts come from the UK and Denmark, and UK Biobank volunteers tend to be healthier than the general population. Results could look different in other countries and groups.
And finally, the only way to know whether treating this group helps is a randomized trial: treat some, give others placebo, and count the heart events. Those trials are still needed.

visual.stock_query: two groups split by coin flip

scenes.narration: The researchers think this makes a case for widening eligibility, but they also say clinical trials are needed first. So on its own, this study can't change who qualifies tomorrow. What it does suggest is that BMI alone may be missing part of the picture.
So what can you do with this today? Quite a lot, starting with a few good questions.
scenes.retention_device: Question re-hook into the practical chapter

scenes.narration: If your BMI is in the mid-twenties and you're curious about your heart risk, here are questions worth bringing to your next appointment.
One. Based on my last cholesterol panel, what's my estimated remnant cholesterol? And are my triglycerides where they should be?
Two. Would a high-sensitivity CRP test add anything for someone like me? And if it comes back high, should we repeat it when I'm well?
Three. What's my overall ten-year heart risk, counting blood pressure, blood sugar, smoking and family history, not just my weight?
Four. Is there anything in my history, like type 2 diabetes or existing cardiovascular disease, that changes which treatment options fit me?
And five. Which changes would move my numbers the most right now?

Here's the encouraging part: these numbers aren't fixed. An American Heart Association statement notes triglycerides often respond well to lifestyle changes, like cutting back on alcohol and added sugar, moving more, and losing extra weight.

And if a GLP-1 medicine ever comes up, remember it's a prescription treatment. The most common side effects are nausea and other stomach symptoms, usually mild to moderate and temporary. Whether it's right for you is a conversation for you and your doctor or prescriber.
scenes.retention_device: Trust builder: side effects and clinician line

scenes.narration: Let's go back to those two people with the same BMI of twenty-six.
On the scale, they're identical. But in their blood, one might carry leftover cholesterol and a slow-burning inflammation signal, with heart risk closer to people who qualify for a GLP-1 today.

visual.stock_query: x-ray style view of two bloodstreams

scenes.narration: That fits a wider shift. A twenty twenty-five Lancet commission argued BMI works as a screening tool, but shouldn't be the only way to judge someone's health.

visual.stock_query: BMI chart beside wider health dashboard

scenes.narration: Here's your checklist. Estimate your remnant cholesterol from your lipid panel. Ask about high-sensitivity CRP, repeated when you're well. Ask for your full ten-year heart risk. And remember: this study didn't test any GLP-1 drug.

items: Ask about hs-CRP, repeated when well
visual.stock_query: checklist with heart and blood drop

scenes.narration: Whether these markers should change who gets GLP-1 medicines is a question for trials, not one conference talk. But knowing your numbers? That can start at your next checkup.

factcheck.summary: Accurate, well-hedged and safe. I checked the core claims against the sources. The EASD 2026 study by Hvid and colleagues matches the reporting: 313,145 adults with BMI 25 or higher and no coronary heart disease or diabetes at baseline, 23,134 cases of coronary heart disease, follow-up of up to 15 years in UK Biobank and 18 in the Copenhagen study, and 44% (Copenhagen) and 48% (UK Biobank) of the BMI 25–26.9 group with high remnant cholesterol, low-grade inflammation or both. The reporting also says this group was "just as likely" to develop coronary heart disease as people already eligible. EASD 2026 runs 28 Sep–2 Oct in Milan. The FDA heart approval (March 2024) and the SELECT figures (6.5% vs 8.0%, 17,604 people) check out. The 2026 US dyslipidemia guideline supports two points: it formally recognizes triglyceride-rich remnant particles, and it treats hs-CRP of 2 mg/L or more and persistent triglycerides of 175 mg/dL or more as risk enhancers. Framing is good throughout: the script says the study is observational and tested no GLP-1 drug, gives relative and absolute risk side by side, calls the remnant estimate rough, includes the "talk to your prescriber" line, and never gives dosing or tells anyone to change medication. The remaining issues are minor wording fixes: the SELECT/FDA population should be "cardiovascular disease", not "heart disease"; the authors' own call to widen eligibility should be stated accurately; and the thresholds need small tweaks for precision and for UK viewers. Apply the fixes below. The remaining S1 references were not re-opened in this pass and are cited from established literature (see the note at the end of the source list).

issues.claim: FDA approved semaglutide ... in adults with established heart disease and either overweight or obesity
issues.problem: The FDA wording is 'adults with cardiovascular disease and either obesity or overweight'. SELECT enrolled people with prior heart attack, stroke or symptomatic peripheral artery disease, so 'heart disease' is too narrow.
issues.fix: Narration: "Then there's a heart approval. In twenty twenty-four, the FDA approved semaglutide to lower the risk of heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death in adults with established cardiovascular disease and either overweight or obesity."

issues.claim: adults aged forty-five or older, with existing heart disease ... / stat label 'adults with heart disease in SELECT'
issues.problem: SELECT required established cardiovascular disease (prior heart attack, stroke or symptomatic peripheral artery disease), not only heart disease.
issues.fix: Narration: "That approval was based on SELECT: a trial of seventeen thousand, six hundred and four adults aged forty-five or older, with established cardiovascular disease, like a past heart attack or stroke, a BMI of twenty-seven or more, and no diabetes." stat_label: "adults with cardiovascular disease in SELECT"

issues.claim: So this study isn't saying eligibility should change tomorrow.
issues.problem: The researchers say their findings make a case for extending GLP-1 eligibility, and they also say clinical trials are now needed. Saying the study 'isn't saying' eligibility should change misstates the authors' position.
issues.fix: Narration: "The researchers think this makes a case for widening eligibility, but they also say clinical trials are needed first. So on its own, this study can't change who qualifies tomorrow. What it does suggest is that BMI alone may be missing part of the picture."

issues.claim: hs-CRP of two milligrams per liter or more, on two separate tests, as a risk-enhancing factor
issues.problem: Summaries of the 2026 guideline describe hs-CRP of 2 mg/L or more on repeated measurements, with no identifiable cause, mainly in people at borderline risk. 'Two separate tests' is slightly more specific than the sources I could reach.
issues.fix: Narration: "Current US cholesterol guidelines treat a high-sensitivity CRP of two milligrams per liter or more, when it stays high on repeat testing with no other explanation, as a risk-enhancing factor." on_screen_text: "hs-CRP 2+ on repeat tests"; stat_label: "hs-CRP on repeat tests: a risk enhancer"

issues.claim: triglycerides that stay at one hundred seventy-five milligrams per deciliter or higher
issues.problem: This is accurate for the guideline's persistent non-fasting threshold, but UK, Canadian and Australian viewers read their results in mmol/L.
issues.fix: stat_label: "persistent triglycerides (about 2 mmol/L): a US risk enhancer". Optionally add to the narration: "that's about two millimoles per liter".

issues.claim: Outside of type 2 diabetes, the main doors into these medicines have a BMI number on them.
issues.problem: 'Main' is a fair hedge, but in 2025 semaglutide was also approved in the US for MASH with fibrosis, and that approval has no BMI cutoff. The sentence is slightly overbroad.
issues.fix: Narration: "Notice the pattern. Outside of type 2 diabetes and a few specific conditions, most doors into these medicines have a BMI number on them. And for a lot of people, the number that matters is twenty-seven."

issues.claim: Take your total cholesterol. Subtract your LDL. Then subtract your HDL.
issues.problem: The formula is correct. Viewers should know it works in either mg/dL or mmol/L, as long as all three numbers use the same unit. The s35 caveat already covers accuracy.
issues.fix: Add to the end of the s34 narration: "Just keep all three numbers in the same units."

thumbnail.reasoning: Candidate #0 ("HIDDEN RISK?") delivers the clearest and most faithful visualization of the title's core tension: two hearts, identically labeled 'BMI 26,' with opposite expressions (worried/red-X vs. happy/green-check). This single-glance contrast is the strongest curiosity hook of the three and requires no extra reading to understand the twist, while the question mark keeps it appropriately hedged rather than sensational. Legibility is excellent at all sizes — the headline is huge and high-contrast, and even the small BMI tags remain readable due to color coding and icon redundancy. Candidate #1 has a good curiosity number ('2 BLOOD TESTS') but its supporting sub-line shrinks to near-illegibility at small thumbnail sizes, and the water-drop mascot doesn't visually connect to 'heart risk.' Candidate #2's headline is more generic and its red-circle decorative element points at an ambiguous target, diluting the focal point. Given the ≥7 legibility bar, #0 is the standout both on CTR potential and clarity, and it best matches the title without overselling the claim.
